s: Some constitutional questions are committed to the political branches or cannot be resolved with judicial standards.
Baker v. Carr (1962) listed six indicators, and the first two do nearly all the work in modern cases.
Baker v. Carr political question factors.
A textually demonstrable constitutional commitment of the issue to a coordinate political department.
A lack of judicially discoverable and manageable standards for resolving it.
The impossibility of deciding without an initial policy determination of a kind clearly for nonjudicial discretion.
The impossibility of a court's independent resolution without expressing lack of the respect due coordinate branches.
An unusual need for unquestioning adherence to a political decision already made.
The potential embarrassment from multifarious pronouncements by various departments on one question.
Guarantee Clause claims are classically nonjusticiable (Luther v. Borden, 1849).
Senate impeachment trial procedures are textually committed to the Senate, which has the "sole Power to try" impeachments (Nixon v. United States, 1993).
Partisan gerrymandering claims present political questions beyond the reach of federal courts for lack of manageable standards (Rucho v. Common Cause, 2019).
Racial gerrymandering and one-person-one-vote claims remain justiciable (Baker; Reynolds).
Foreign affairs cases are not automatically political.
In Zivotofsky v. Clinton (2012), whether a statute about passport birthplaces was constitutional was a familiar question of statutory and constitutional interpretation.
